```{r forest, fig.height = 6.5}
md <- sapply(dd, mean); sd_ <- sapply(dd, sem); o <- order(md)
par(mar = c(4, 19, 3, 1))
plot(md[o], seq_along(o), pch = 19, yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlim = range(c(md - 2 * sd_, md + 2 * sd_, 0)),
     xlab = "MSPE minus GBLUP MSPE (positive = worse than GBLUP; +-2 SE)", main = "Every method against full-SNP GBLUP")
```

The ten splits reuse the same accessions, so these standard errors describe split-to-split variation only and are
optimistic; read the ordering and the size of the gaps, not the nominal significance.

## 12.2 Key findings (computed from the results above)

```{r key-findings, results='asis'}
R2 <- function(v) mean(1 - v / base_s[names(v)])
gm <- gbn
a <- named(si, "RP_agg"); dga <- a - gm[names(a)]
cat(sprintf("1. **TARP claims reproduced.** One random projection: MSPE %.1f; 100-draw aggregation: %.1f; exact PCA: %.1f; mean-only: %.1f. Aggregated TARP matches PCA (difference %.1f, SE %.1f).\n",
            mean(si$RP_single), mean(si$RP_agg), mean(si$PCA), mean(si$baseline), mean(si$RP_agg - si$PCA), sem(si$RP_agg - si$PCA)))
cat(sprintf("2. **Dense baseline wins.** Full-SNP GBLUP R-squared %.3f versus aggregated TARP %.3f; GBLUP better by %.1f MSPE (SE %.1f), in %d of %d splits.\n",
            R2(gm), R2(a), mean(dga), sem(dga), sum(dga > 0), length(dga)))
cat(sprintf("3. **SIS family.** Best SIS-based recipe: `%s` (R-squared %.3f); hard SIS with d = n/log n is too small here (%.3f). Structure-adjusted SIS plus ancestry axes: %.3f.\n",
            names(which.max(sapply(r2s[grepl("SIS", names(r2s))], mean))), max(sapply(r2s[grepl("SIS", names(r2s))], mean)),
            if ("SIS d = 120 + lasso" %in% names(r2s)) mean(r2s[["SIS d = 120 + lasso"]]) else NA,
            if ("Structure-adjusted SIS + lasso + axes" %in% names(r2s)) mean(r2s[["Structure-adjusted SIS + lasso + axes"]]) else NA))
cat(sprintf("4. **Pitfalls.** Test labels in screening make RIS-PCR look %.0f%% better than it is; tuning after screening picks median log10(lambda) %.1f (LOOCV) versus %.2f (nested CV) and %.1f without screening.\n",
            100 * (1 - mean(leak$PCA_leaky) / mean(si$PCA)), median(log10(e1$lam_lin_loo)), median(log10(e1b$lam_lin)), median(log10(e0$lam_lin_loo))))
cat(sprintf("5. **Structure.** Relatedness-only predictors reach R-squared %.3f (nearest relatives) and %.3f (LCA classes, K = 8) against %.3f for GBLUP; GBLUP's within-class correlation is %.2f at K = 8.\n",
            R2(named(struct, "NW")), R2(named(struct, "class_only")), R2(gm), wtab$GBLUP_r[wtab$K == 8]))
cat(sprintf("6. **Targeted GBLUP** minus GBLUP: %.2f (SE %.2f); group screening versus individual screening with PCA: %.2f (SE %.2f). Neither adds detectable accuracy on FT10.\n",
            mean(e3$TwoK_honest - e3$GBLUP_nested), sem(e3$TwoK_honest - e3$GBLUP_nested),
            mean(grp_res$GSIS_PCA - grp_res$RIS_PCA), sem(grp_res$GSIS_PCA - grp_res$RIS_PCA)))
cat(sprintf("7. **Intervals.** Nominal 90%% coverage: TARP-style %.3f (PCA) and %.3f (random projection); GBLUP split-conformal %.3f; Mondrian-by-ancestry worst-cluster coverage %.3f.\n",
            mean(e2$cov_E_TARP_PCA_NIG), mean(e2$cov_F_TARP_RP_NIG), mean(e2$cov_A_conformal), mean(e2$mincov_D_mondrian)))
f16 <- tr_rows[tr_rows$Trait == "FT16", ]
cat(sprintf("8. **Second trait (FT16).** Same ordering: as a percentage of GBLUP's MSPE, targeted GBLUP %.1f%%, honest screened ridge %+.1f%%, aggregated TARP %+.1f%%.\n",
            f16$Pct_of_GBLUP_MSPE[f16$Method == "TGB"], f16$Pct_of_GBLUP_MSPE[f16$Method == "SCR"], f16$Pct_of_GBLUP_MSPE[f16$Method == "AGG"]))
```

## 12.3 What can and cannot be claimed

**Supported by these experiments**

- TARP's aggregation requirement, and the rough equivalence of aggregated TARP and PCA projection, are reproduced on a
  real dataset with p of about 1.7 million.
- Classical SIS, randomized SIS, iterated SIS and structure-adjusted SIS were implemented and compared. Screening
  recovers loci, not individual SNPs (LD), is pulled toward ancestry-tagging SNPs when ancestry drives the phenotype, and
  that pull is reduced by adjusting for ancestry before screening (simulation, Section 5.3).
- On FT10 and FT16, full-SNP GBLUP is at least as accurate as every screening-based method tried; targeted GBLUP is
  statistically tied with it.
- Leakage and tuning after supervised screening are biased and nested tuning fixes it; intervals built after screening
  under-cover; conformal intervals around GBLUP are calibrated.
- GBLUP predicts within lineages, not only between them.

**Not supported, do not claim**

- A new method that beats GBLUP or TARP.
- Nonlinearity or epistasis (the Gaussian-kernel edge appeared only after screening and vanished without it).
- That random-projection intervals cover better than PCA intervals (within noise).
- Novelty for conformal prediction, Mondrian calibration, ancestry-explicit models, latent-class mixtures or mixture
  priors: all are established, so their role here is application and quantification.
- That group screening helps (it did not, with this LD proxy).
- Generality beyond flowering time until a trait with a different genetic architecture has been run.

# 13. Discussion

**Replication.** The mechanics of TARP (soft screening, sparse random projection, closed-form NIG fit, aggregation) work as
described. A single projection is not a usable estimator; the paper's aggregation is essential, and with it the method
matches PCA projection. Randomized SVD with TARP's own sketch is a cheaper way to the same accuracy than 100
aggregated projections, though not cheaper than exact PCA through the Gram matrix when n is small.

**Screening and variable selection.** Marginal screening ranks SNPs one at a time. In genetic data this has three
consequences, each measured here: strong LD means one causal locus is represented by many near-duplicate SNPs, so the
selected set is large but covers few loci and exact recovery is poor while locus recovery is good; ancestry that drives
the phenotype makes ancestry-tagging SNPs rank highly, and screening the ancestry-adjusted response removes that pull;
and a hard cut-off of n/log n is far too small for a trait with many contributing loci. The soft, randomized rule of
TARP keeps a much larger set and loses little relative to hard SIS of the same size, so the budget matters more than the
randomization.

**Does structure help?** In two different senses. For *variable selection*, adjusting for ancestry before screening
changes what is selected in the intended direction. For *prediction*, the useful structure is the genome-wide similarity
between accessions that a dense kernel exploits automatically: it explains most of the predictable signal, an explicit
ancestry component adds nothing to it, and structure-based group screening (with an LD proxy) did not help either. The
practical reading is that for a polygenic trait the structure is best used by modeling all SNPs jointly rather than by
selecting a few.

**Calibration.** Screening on the response and then quoting model-based intervals double-counts the data; calibrated
intervals need either a calibration set untouched by screening (split conformal) or an analysis that accounts for the
selection. Coverage is the one place where the dense model's advantage is not about accuracy but about trust.

**Limitations.** One organism and two strongly correlated flowering traits; n of about 1,000 (a regime where an n x n
dense kernel is cheap, which favors GBLUP; at much larger n and p screening and projection regain their computational
role); ten splits of the same accessions; LD blocks proxied by clustering and positions rather than a gene annotation;
the group-screening code implements only the GSIS statistic; approximate gene coordinates for FRI and FLC in the
Manhattan plot are typed from memory and must be checked before citing.

**Next steps.** (i) A trait dominated by a few large-effect loci (Section 11) to locate the regime where screening
beats dense kernels; (ii) a consistency analysis for structure-aware projection (the open piece of the TARP theory),
motivated by the equivalence of aggregated random projection and PCA seen here; (iii) LD-aware grouping from a gene
annotation; (iv) larger samples, where screening is computationally necessary.
